title: Other Grammar Topics
intro: Check adjectives, adverbs, comparisons, and common grammar traps.

sections.heading: Commonly confused word pairs
body: Match the word’s job: their = belonging to them; there = place; they’re = they are. Your and its show ownership; you’re = you are; it’s = it is or it has.
Affect usually means influence; effect usually means result. Accept means receive; except means other than. Whose shows ownership; who’s means who is or who has. Expand shortened forms to test them.
Principle means a rule; principal can mean main. Complement completes or suits something; compliment praises it.
Past can be a preposition; passed is a past-tense verb.

examples.text: The storm will affect traffic, and its main effect is delay.
examples.label: affect = verb, its = possessive, effect = noun

examples.text: The storm will effect traffic, and it's main affect is delay.
examples.label: All three swapped: effect for affect, it's for its, affect for effect

examples.text: The cool sauce complements the hot dish; the chef accepted the diner’s compliment.
examples.label: Complement means go well with; compliment means praise.

sections.tip: Expand contractions: it’s = it is or it has; who’s = who is or who has; they’re = they are. If no expansion fits, check whether the sentence needs possession or a plain word such as there.

sections.heading: Than vs. then, and could have vs. could of
body: Than compares; then marks time or sequence. Identify which relationship the sentence needs.
Write could have, should have, and would have. Could’ve sounds like “could of,” but the verb construction requires have, not of.

examples.text: She runs faster than I do, so I should have trained harder.
examples.label: than for comparison, have after should

examples.text: She runs faster then I do, so I should of trained harder.
examples.label: then and 'should of' are both wrong

sections.tip: The verb phrases are could have, should have, and would have. Of cannot replace have in those auxiliary-plus-participle constructions.

sections.heading: Countable vs. non-countable words
body: For separately countable items, use fewer, number, or many: fewer chairs, many students.
For an amount treated as a mass, use less, amount, or much: less water, much information. Check how the noun is being used in the sentence.

examples.text: The recipe needs fewer eggs and a smaller amount of sugar.
examples.label: fewer with countable eggs, amount with mass-noun sugar

examples.text: The recipe needs less eggs and a smaller number of sugar.
examples.label: less and number attached to the wrong noun types

sections.tip: Can you put a number directly in front of the noun (three eggs)? Use fewer, number, many. If you can't (three sugars makes no sense here), use less, amount, much.

sections.heading: Active vs. passive voice
body: Active voice makes the actor the subject: “The committee approved the plan.” Passive voice makes the receiver the subject: “The plan was approved.”
Passive voice is grammatical. Prefer the clearer, more concise choice when meaning and emphasis stay appropriate; do not reject passive voice automatically.
Avoid an unmotivated voice shift inside a sequence of one actor’s actions; keep that actor as the shared subject.

examples.text: The plan was approved yesterday; the committee will implement it Monday.
examples.label: Passive keeps the plan as the topic; the next clause changes to the actor

examples.text: The plan was approved by the committee.
examples.label: Grammatical passive: use it when the plan is the focus

examples.text: The technician sorted the samples, checked their labels, and recorded their masses.
examples.label: The shared actor remains the subject throughout the active verb sequence.

sections.tip: Choose voice to serve the passage: actor first for emphasis on responsibility, receiver first when it is the continuing topic.

sections.heading: Prepositional idioms
body: Learn standard pairings in context: interested in, capable of, depend on, comply with, consist of, responsible for, prefer X to Y, and different from.
Agree with a person or opinion; agree to a plan or terms. When choices vary only the preposition, check the phrase’s intended meaning and construction.
Prefer X to Y and rather X than Y. Compare matching forms: interested in drawing more than in painting.
Divide items among recipients.

examples.text: Her method differs from mine, but I agree with her goal.
examples.label: differ from; agree with an opinion

examples.text: Her method differs of mine, but I agree at her goal.
examples.label: These prepositions do not fit the intended constructions

examples.text: The device is capable of recording changes while complying with the laboratory’s rules.
examples.label: Capable of takes an -ing form; comply with introduces the rule.

sections.tip: Learn the complete construction. Different from is standard, and different than also occurs in American English; do not invent an error based on a disputed blanket ban.

sections.heading: How to spot these questions
body: Identify the change: sound-alike, countable/mass word, preposition, or voice.

Expand shortened words, check whether the noun can be counted, test the usual word pairing, or compare clarity and meaning. Use the rule that matches the question instead of choosing only by familiarity.
sections.tip: Check what changes: grammatical role, meaning, word pairing, or tone. Apply that specific test; a one-word change can concern style as well as grammar.

sections.heading: Advanced transfer: comparisons and adjective/adverb roles
body: Compare corresponding things: the budget for restoration was larger than the budget for storage, or larger than that for storage. Do not compare a budget directly with a department or building.

A linking verb describes its subject with an adjective: the sample looks clear. An action verb may need an adverb: the technician labeled it clearly. For comparisons, use a comparative for two and a superlative for a set of three or more.

examples.text: The north wing's roof is steeper than that of the south wing.
examples.label: That replaces roof, keeping roof compared with roof.

examples.text: The north wing's roof is steeper than the south wing.
examples.label: The wording compares a roof with an entire wing instead of the corresponding roof.

examples.text: The recording sounded faint even though the engineer had labeled every track clearly.
examples.label: Faint describes recording after the linking verb sounded; clearly modifies the action labeled.

sections.tip: Ask what is being compared and what the describing word actually modifies.

sections.heading: Use comparative and superlative forms for the stated comparison
body: Use a comparative when directly comparing two: clearer than, the better of the two. Use a superlative to select the extreme within a set of three or more: the clearest of five. Avoid doubled forms such as more clearer or most easiest.

Good/better/best and bad/worse/worst are irregular. Longer adjectives often use more or most. For an action, compare adverbs: she explained it more clearly, not more clear. The group size and the word’s grammatical job both matter.

examples.text: Of the two drafts, the second is clearer. Of the six submitted drafts, it is the clearest.
examples.label: The comparison is between two in the first sentence and selects the extreme of a larger set in the second.

examples.text: The technician measured the second sample more carefully than the first.
examples.label: More carefully is a comparative adverb describing measured; more careful would be an adjective.

check.stem: If you study tonight, [[your]] going to feel ready for the test.
check.explanation: Expand the contraction: 'you are going to feel ready' works, so 'you're' is correct. 'Your' is a possessive and would need a noun to own, 'yours' is a standalone possessive that cannot sit before 'going,' and 'their' is both possessive and the wrong person.

check.stem: We packed [[less]] sandwiches than we did last year.
check.explanation: Sandwiches can be counted, so the comparison needs 'fewer.' 'Less' and 'much' pair with non-countable nouns like 'bread,' and 'lesser' means lower in quality or rank, not smaller in number.

check.stem: The new rule will [[effect]] every student who rides the bus.
check.explanation: The sentence needs a verb meaning to influence, which is 'affect.' 'Effect' is usually a noun (a result); its rare verb sense, 'to bring about,' makes no sense with 'every student' as the object. The helping verb 'will' must be followed by a base form, so the -s forms 'effects' and 'affects' cannot follow it.
